title: Browser Security Basics
summary: Frontend code runs in a browser that handles private user data and untrusted input.

subtopics.title: Untrusted input
subtopics.explanation: Text from a user, URL, or outside service may contain content an attacker controls. Display it as text and validate it before sensitive use. It is like reading a note without letting it issue commands. Decide what formats and lengths your application accepts. In practice, render a user’s comment as text instead of concatenating it into an HTML string. In a real page, render comments as text so markup from a user is not interpreted as code.

subtopics.title: Cross-site scripting
subtopics.explanation: Cross-site scripting (XSS) happens when attacker-controlled content runs as code in a trusted page. Use safe rendering, avoid unsafe HTML insertion, and apply a carefully tested Content Security Policy. It is like preventing a visitor’s note from being treated as an official instruction. Fix the unsafe input path first; a policy is an added defense. In practice, a CSP can limit script sources, but it does not repair unsafe application logic. In a real page, test CSP changes in report-only mode before enforcing a policy that may block needed scripts.

subtopics.title: Cross-site request forgery
subtopics.explanation: Cross-site request forgery (CSRF) tricks a signed-in browser into sending an unwanted request. Server protections such as SameSite cookies and anti-CSRF tokens help stop it. It is like someone forging an order using a trusted courier. The server must verify that a sensitive action was intentionally requested. In practice, protect a state-changing request on the server even when a cookie is SameSite. In a real page, require a CSRF check for a cookie-authenticated state change.

subtopics.title: Browser boundaries
subtopics.explanation: The same-origin policy limits how one site can read another site’s data. CORS lets a server grant selected cross-origin access; it is not a frontend switch that makes private APIs secure. It is like a receptionist checking which visitors may enter a room. Configure allowed origins on the server and still authenticate users. In practice, allow a trusted origin only when the API needs cross-origin browser access. In a real page, configure CORS on the API server and permit only known origins.

subtopics.title: Secrets and authorization
subtopics.explanation: Anything shipped to the browser can be inspected. Keep secrets on servers, and have the server check permission for every protected action. Hiding a button only changes the interface. It is like hiding a door sign without locking the room. Test unauthorized requests directly against the server. In practice, try a protected endpoint without the interface to confirm the server rejects unauthorized requests. In a real page, call an endpoint directly without a button to verify server authorization.

foundations.overview: Browser security protects users when a page handles data, accounts, and outside content. Treat user input and network responses as untrusted, keep secrets on servers, and make the server check permission for protected actions. Think of the browser as a public room: visitors can inspect what runs there. Safe rendering, careful cross-origin rules, and server-side checks reduce risk but do not replace a full security review.
foundations.whyItMatters: Browser defenses depend on safe rendering, controlled origins, and server authorization. Security controls should be tested against actual attack paths, not inferred from the interface.
foundations.browserPerspective: The browser enforces origin rules, cookie policies, and security headers alongside application behavior.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Review input handling, cookies, redirects, content policy, and server authorization.
foundations.businessImpact: Security failures can expose accounts and private data, damaging user trust.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Use a defense-in-depth review across browser, server, and deployment settings.
foundations.performanceImpact: Limit third-party scripts and keep dependencies updated.
commonUseCases: Render rich user content only through a trusted sanitization path.
Review third-party scripts because they execute in the page security context.

commonMisconceptions.reality: Users can change browser code; the server must enforce access.
CORS controls some reads; it does not replace CSRF or authorization defenses.

keyTakeaways: Text from a user, URL, or outside service may contain content an attacker controls.
Cross-site scripting (XSS) happens when attacker-controlled content runs as code in a trusted page.
Cross-site request forgery (CSRF) tricks a signed-in browser into sending an unwanted request.
The same-origin policy limits how one site can read another site’s data.
Anything shipped to the browser can be inspected.
